text: There again, Socrates, I think you speak the truth.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: So that right opinion will be no whit inferior to knowledge in worth or usefulness as regards our actions, nor will the man who has right opinion be inferior to him who has knowledge.
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: That is so.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: And you know that the good man has been admitted by us to be useful.
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: Since then it is not only because of knowledge that men will be good and useful to their country, where such men are to be found, but also on account of right opinion; and since neither of these two things—knowledge
and true opinion—is a natural property of mankind, being acquired—or do you think that either of them is natural?
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Not I.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: Then if they are not natural, good people cannot be good by nature either.
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Of course not.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: And since they are not an effect of nature, we next considered whether virtue can be taught.
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: And we thought it teachable if virtue is wisdom?
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: And if teachable, it must be wisdom?
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: And if there were teachers, it could be taught,
but if there were none, it could not?
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Quite so.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: But surely we acknowledged that it had no teachers?
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: That is true.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: Then we acknowledged it neither was taught nor was wisdom?
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: But yet we admitted it was a good?
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: And that which guides rightly is useful and good?
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: And that there are only two things—

true opinion and knowledge—that guide rightly and a man guides rightly if he have these; for things that come about by chance do not occur through human guidance; but where a man is a guide to what is right we find these two things—true opinion and knowledge.
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: I agree.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: Well now, since virtue is not taught, we no longer take it to be knowledge?
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Apparently not.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: So of two good and useful things one has been rejected: knowledge cannot be our guide in political conduct.
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: I think not.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: Therefore it was not by any wisdom, nor because they were wise, that the sort of men we spoke of controlled their states—Themistocles and the rest of them, to whom our friend Anytus was referring a moment ago. For this reason it was that they were unable to make others like unto themselves—because their qualities were not an effect of knowledge.
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: The case is probably as you say, Socrates.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: And if not by knowledge, as the only alternative it must have been by good opinion.

This is the means which statesmen employ for their direction of states, and they have nothing more to do with wisdom than soothsayers and diviners; for these people utter many a true thing when inspired, but have no knowledge of anything they say.
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: I daresay that is so.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: And may we, Meno, rightly call those men divine who, having no understanding, yet succeed in many a great deed and word?
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: Then we shall be right in calling those divine of whom

we spoke just now as soothsayers and prophets and all of the poetic turn; and especially we can say of the statesmen that they are divine and enraptured, as being inspired and possessed of God when they succeed in speaking many great things, while knowing nought of what they say.
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: And the women too, I presume, Meno, call good men divine; and the Spartans, when they eulogize a good man, say—“He is a divine person.”
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: And to all appearance, Socrates, they are right; though perhaps our friend Anytus may be annoyed at your statement.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: For my part, I care not. As for him, Meno, we will converse with him some other time. At the moment, if through all this discussion our queries and statements have been correct, virtue is found to be neither natural nor taught, but is imparted to us by a divine dispensation without understanding in those who receive it,

unless there should be somebody among the statesmen capable of making a statesman of another. And if there should be any such, he might fairly be said to be among the living what Homer says Teiresias was among the dead—“He alone has comprehension; the rest are flitting shades.” In the same way he on earth, in respect of virtue, will be a real substance among shadows.
blocks.speaker: Socrates

text: I think you put it excellently, Socrates.
blocks.speaker: Meno

text: Then the result of our reasoning, Meno, is found to be that virtue comes to us by a divine dispensation, when it does come. But the certainty of this we shall only know when, before asking in what way virtue comes to mankind, we set about inquiring what virtue is, in and by itself. It is time now for me to go my way, but do you persuade our friend Anytus of that whereof you are now yourself persuaded, so as
to put him in a gentler mood; for if you can persuade him, you will do a good turn to the people of Athens also.
blocks.speaker: Socrates
